The xiao, also called dongxiao, changxiao or xiaoguan, is an ancient Chinese aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.221.12: a single end-blown open pipe sounded by an edge tone. The tube is mostly bamboo, commonly purple bamboo, though solid wood is also hollowed out; the blowing edge may be cut U-shaped, V-shaped or in the Tang style, the fingerholes are traditionally six and nowadays often eight, and there are further vent holes at the bottom. In playing the tube stands at about forty-five degrees to the body, and the common key is G, with F as well. Players often use it for solos, for duets with the guqin and in silk-and-bamboo music, and it also appears in regional music such as the nanyin of Quanzhou.
簫多以竹製成，常見紫竹（黑竹），亦有桂竹、孟宗竹、石竹；部分以實木鑿空。管身可素: The xiao is mostly made of bamboo, commonly purple bamboo (black bamboo), but also makino bamboo, Moso bamboo and dwarf bamboo; some are hollowed from solid wood. The tube may be left plain, or given horn inlay or carving at the end. It is often bound with nylon line to steady the bamboo and keep it from splitting. The blowing edge may be undercut U-shaped, V-shaped or at a slant, sometimes with bone or ivory inlay; metal rings may be fitted between the blowing edge and the fingerholes and between the last hole and the tail end, for tuning or for taking the instrument apart to carry. Southern xiao often keep the bamboo root, and those used in Taiwan are mostly made of Taiwanese bamboo.
簫為中國古老氣鳴吹管樂器，單管、豎吹、開管、以邊稜音發聲，起源常與古代西南羌人的: The xiao is an ancient Chinese aerophone: a single end-blown open pipe sounded by an edge tone, its origin often linked to the end-blown flutes of the ancient Qiang of the south-west. Before the Han, both side-blown and end-blown pipes could be called di; the end-blown di described in Ma Rong's “Rhapsody on the Long Flute” had four holes, and Jing Fang of the Western Han added a back hole, which is already close to the dongxiao that has come down to us. Before the Tang the word xiao mostly meant the panpipe; after the Tang and Song the single end-blown pipe became current, and the panpipe was kept distinct by its own name. In the Tang an end-blown instrument one chi eight cun long was called chiba (shakuhachi), and it was carried to Japan. Yuan banquet music records a five-hole xiao, and after the Ming and Qing the instrument is linked to court ritual music and to silk-and-bamboo playing; in the twentieth century Peng Zhiqing made an eight-hole ya-xiao, also called qin-xiao, which suits playing with the guqin and has shaped today's eight-hole xiao.
簫為氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 421.221.12，單管豎吹、: The xiao is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.221.12: a single end-blown open pipe sounded by the edge tone at the blowing edge. On the common G xiao the lowest note, with all holes closed, is the D above middle C, and there are F instruments as well; six or eight holes mainly affect the convenience of fingering and do not widen the range. The short, stout southern xiao has a deep, thick tone; the slender northern xiao and the qin-xiao have a smaller bore and lower volume, so their tone is softer and suits playing with the guqin, whereas an ordinary northern xiao easily drowns the guqin. Volume depends on the bore and on breath control, and the shorter instruments need more precise control.
簫（421.221.12）為氣鳴樂器，屬東亞中國豎吹簫，常見於獨奏、琴簫合奏、絲: The xiao (421.221.12) is an aerophone, the end-blown Chinese flute of East Asia; it is common in solo playing, in qin-and-xiao duets and in silk-and-bamboo music, and in the nanguan theatre music of Quanzhou in Fujian; it also appears in court ritual music. The qin-xiao has a slender tube and a softer tone and is played with the guqin; the southern xiao belongs to nanguan, and the northern xiao is the common variant of the north.
